questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Other

questions.question: Please explain: *
questions.answer: My primary motivation for going on exchange was the opportunity to travel combined with the character development that entails. To be able to explore new horizons while also being able to study in a different manner was very appealling to me.

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I have always wanted to experience Australia because of its beautiful, grand and very different nature, because of the possibility of surfing and because of the friendly reputation the people there has. It was also important for me to go to an English speaking country because I think I would feel more isolated if I was not able to speak the native tongue. I wanted to choose a bigger city because I wanted to be a part of a larger exchange-student community. All of those factors made me choose the University of Sydney.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Even though I have rated my experience quite high, I would like to add that it is not always smooth sailing. I felt that the application, visa, and preparation phase was difficult with the amount of help available which was frustrating at times. A tip is that it is very nice to be in contact with people who have gone through the same process before you. Being on exchange far from home also comes with its practical and mental challenges. And one thing I think is important to remember is that whatever you might struggle with back home will not disappear when you go on exchange. It might even become more clear to you which I actually think is a good thing but also a thing worth knowing.
All that being said, I am very glad that I went and I would gladly do the entire thing again.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I thought some of the information was hard to find especially regarding visa, but I also had three changes of advisors from my exchange university in the semester leading up to my departure. I felt like they were sometimes bad at guiding me and they didn't answer my questions specificly enough. The response time was usually a bit slow. I often felt like I got the most help from students who had gone to Sydney on exchange before me.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Other than e-mails I had an opportunity to get an in-person drop-in session with my advisor which I took, and that was really helpful (much more so than the e-mails).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I came a little late, so I missed some of the social introductory events. I felt like there should have been more of those but since I could not attend the ones two weeks prior to the semester start it is hard for me to comment on the overall orientation. I would advise people to get to Sydney at least two weeks before semester start, so they can settle in socially before classes start, however it is not paramount.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
You get sent a list over possible student accomodation in Sydney from the university. If you do not want to deal with the hassle of finding a place on you own I would recommend just applying for one of those places as quickly as possible because they do get filled up relatively quickly. They are not the only possible choices though but most "student accomodations" in that area are similar I think. In generel the rent is ridiculously overpriced.
I lived in the Queen Mary Building (QMB) which I liked. You only get a small room without your own bathroom or kitchen, but the building is very social and have everything you need. It is located right beside the campus. It is also very easy to meet a lot of cool people there.
It is still too pricey but it is the cheapest option of the overpriced student accomodations, and therefore I can really recommend the QMB despite its flaws.
If you want to find a place on your own, I think you might be able to find much better accomodation than the university offers but it is definitely a bigger task and you are probably not guaranteed to find something better or cheaper so if you want to do that, I would definitely recommend speaking with someone who has tried that before you.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Maybe my accomodation counts as livining on campus because it was right next to it, so I don't know how qualified I am to speak on that. But when I was studying there they had a lot of options for watching lectures and other classes online, so if you want to live further away from campus it might be a good idea to ask how much is online. But I liked living right beside campus so I could easily get to clase when I needed to.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I thought that the housing in it self was more than fine however not anything fancy but it is way too expensive. I feel like they really take advantage of the fact that exchange students desperately need a place to stay for a fixed period of time and have no contacts or knowledge of the place they are going to. So for that reason I cannot say that I am satisfied with the housing available. If the prices became more resonable I would be happy with the accommodation.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I thought the visa process was very tricky because the Sydney advisors are not allowed to help you with it.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Once you had to register for classes they sent you a list of units that you could go through which made it easier to find classes of interest.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You have a study-abroad advisor, that you can write to over e-mail. I thought it was a little frustrating that everything was by e-mail. I don't remember if I requested it, but today I would have probably requested to talk with them on Zoom or over the phone if I had to. But that might not be something that they will do.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Pretty successful as I recall. I changed a couple once I got there but I had gotten forhåndsgodkendelser for a handfull of units I was interested in, which made it easier to change.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Get forhåndsgodkendelser for more units than you need so if you think a class might be wrong for you once the semester has startet it is easier and more carefree to change.
Get help from students who have already been on exchange the same place.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: How good the teaching was really depended on the proffessors

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Level 1000 is first year, 2000 is second year and so on. However we got recommended to do 2000 units even when it was our 3. semester because apparently they are a bit ahead, but I think you can also do 3000 units. I would advise to do a mixture between 2000 and 3000 so you don't get too much work because it is extra heavy when you also have to adjust to living in a different country.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
It was more supportive I think. There were more in-semester assignments and quizzes that counted towards the final grade. I personally quite enjoyed that because it made it easier to follow along and made the final exam less nerve-racking. In my units there were some quite cheap points to get as well which was nice. You do not have to be as controling of your own learning as you do in UCPH.
This might have been because of covid, but all lectures and classes were not only streamed online but also recorded and put up on canvas, which I found really helpful. I think they are going to do that even after covid, because we did have classes where you could meet up in person, where they also streamed and recorded most activities.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
MIMI2002: Microbes, Infection and Immunity
BIOS2171: Human Neuroscience in Health and Disease
BCMB3003: Biochemistry of Human Disease
EDUH4052: Learning in Outdoor Education

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Definitely EDUH4052 because it is a good way of getting to know other exchange students and you get to go on two very cool field trips were you explore some of the beautiful nature around Sydney. It is not a very difficult course so it also frees up time to explore Sydney and work more on your other courses. Hugh recommendation for this course.
MIMI2002 had a great structure and great professors. They both stopped this semester but hopefully their replacements are going to run the course in a similar way. I think it was a fine introduction to the immune system but there is a lot of focus on bacteria, vira and specific diseases which the name also indicates. One of the reasons why I picked it, was because I heard that it was nice to have had some immunology before Humanfysiologi.
BIOS2171 was a good introduction to the nervous system even though I wasn't too thrilled by the professors. However they were really sweat, which was nice.
BCMB3003 was not greatly structured and the in-semester exam (a half-way point exam that counts for a smaller fraction of the final mark than the final exam) was very difficult because the professor responsible for the course didn't seem to have the best idea of what his students knew. It was stressful at times with lab-reports requiring more work than the marks awarded for them suggested, but I thought the topics in the lectures were quite interesting.
Overall I was happy with my courses, however you might be able to find better once and it obviously also depends on interests.

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *

Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
The visa application is quite expensive. I  think it was 3000 and something DKK.
I haven't included cost of traveling but that is obviously one of the most expensive things. Well worth it though. I used 10.000 DKK on a group tour to the East coast on spring break and I do not know I much I used after the semester ended but it wasn't cheap.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: The prices in Sydney are generally a little higher than in Copenhagen. I found that a few items were cheaper. For example milk.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I did not take advantage of it myself but they have a huge amount of clubs for all kinds of different activities or interests. When you arrive you feel like you have all the time in the world to experience Sydney but it all goes by faster than you might expect, so I would advise that if you find a society that you think sounds interesting just join it immidiately. You can always find another one if you end up not liking it.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Too many to mention. They had a chocolate society. I never did, but I should have joined the bush-walking society.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Bush-walking society even though I wasn't a part of it. I met a lot of people that I really liked late in the semester who had all been a part of that, and I think bushwalking is a good way of exploring Australian nature.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Make sure to go on weekend trips to different places in and around Sydney. I liked the beach walk from Bondi beach to Coogee beach. You can take surf lessons on Bondi or Manly beach however I would recommend going on a surfcamp. They will probably get advertised to you. Blue Mountains National Park and Royal National Park are really worth a visit (also more than one). You are going to those two with EDUH4052 if you take that class. 8-figure pools and mermaid pools are some places to visit in Royal national park. I never went there but palm beach in north Sydney should also be cool. Some of the popular clubs in Sydney are Scary Canary, Ivy and Club 77.
On longer holidays I would recommend visiting the East coast of Australia. I personally went from Brisbane to Cairns. Also Uluru in the red center of Australia, Tasmania, Melbourne and the great ocean road, and Byron Bay are all very cool places. I heard a lot of good things about the nature of the west coast too, but I never went there.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: The culture is very western so it was relatively easy. There is a couple of things that you have to get used to still, but it is only nice that it is a little bit different. I felt as if it was more open and friendly than back home.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Just be open and friendly. They most likely will be. And if you find someone you click with invite them for a trip to the beach or for a drink. Remember you only have 4-6 months and you have nothing to lose.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Almost everyone (also other exchange students) will ask "How are you doing" or "How is it going" whenever they see you just as a formality. Sometimes I would start telling them how I was actually doing while all they were looking for was a simple "Good. You?"

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Probably the friendliness.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Treasure your time there and remember that it goes by quicker than you think.
When you meet nice people be sure to use time with them.
See Australia. It is not every day that you are on the other side of the globe.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: There probably is, but I can't come to think of anything right now, but therefore I will suggest to get in contact with someone who has been there before, so that you have someone you can ask all the questions you might have.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The people I got to know well and travel with after the semester had ended.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: It can feel lonely at times when you are that far from home and most people you know. Fortunately, University of Sydney is such a big university that other students from your course most likely will also be there, and that can be very helpfull in that regard.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Sometimes you will hear only good things about people's experiences with exchange and I feel like it is important to tell that it is also challenging and at times tedious (applications and practical stuff) or difficult (mentally) but the rewarding side is so much greater than the efforts made. I would do it again in a heartbeat, and I am very happy that I went.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
